opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and I think it's one of the more open areas right now. So if you look at the recipe that got popular with DeepSeek-R1 and the models that followed, a lot of the success came from using verifiable rewards: you have a math problem with a known answer, or code that either passes the unit tests or doesn't, and you reward the model based on that. That's attractive because it's simple, it's hard to game compared to a learned reward model, and it scales well.

But the limitation is that final-answer correctness is a pretty sparse signal. The model can arrive at the right answer through a flawed chain of reasoning, sometimes by luck or by some shortcut, and it still gets the full reward. And conversely, it might do ninety percent of the reasoning correctly, make one arithmetic slip at the end, and get nothing. So I think there's a lot of interest in rewards that look at the process itself.

Process reward models are one direction. The idea has been around for a while, there was that "Let's Verify Step by Step" work from OpenAI, but in practice they've been tricky. Labeling intermediate steps is expensive, and if you train a model to judge steps, you reintroduce the reward hacking problem. The policy can learn to write steps that look good to the judge without actually being better reasoning. So I'm a bit cautiously optimistic there. I think they'll help, but probably more as one component rather than a replacement for outcome-based rewards.

Then there are the more practical, almost mundane rewards that I think will matter quite a bit. Format rewards were already part of the R1 setup, making sure the model puts its reasoning in the right tags and so forth. Length-related rewards are getting more attention too, because these models have a tendency to overthink. They'll produce really long reasoning traces even for easy problems, and that's expensive at inference time. So penalizing unnecessary length, or rewarding efficiency, is something I expect to see more of. There's also language consistency, where the model would otherwise switch between languages mid-reasoning, which DeepSeek specifically addressed.

And then I think a big frontier is extending this beyond domains where you can easily verify answers. Math and code are nice because you have ground truth, but a lot of what we want from these models, like writing, analysis, or open-ended problem solving, doesn't have a single correct answer. So there you're looking at things like rubric-based rewards, LLM-as-a-judge setups, or checking for consistency and faithfulness. That's harder, and again you have to be careful about the model exploiting the judge.

So my overall expectation is that final-answer correctness stays the backbone, because it's robust, but we'll layer additional signals on top: process signals, efficiency, formatting, and maybe some judgment-based rewards for the fuzzier domains. The trick is balancing them so the model doesn't just optimize the easiest-to-game term. I think a lot of the progress in the next while will come from getting that reward design right, rather than from changes to the RL algorithm itself.

r001.rationale: The response says format rewards ensure the model puts its reasoning in the right tags.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes sparse final-answer correctness rewards from process rewards that assess intermediate reasoning steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's actually one of the more interesting open directions right now. So just to set the stage: most of the reasoning-model work we've seen, DeepSeek-R1 being the canonical example, uses a very simple reward. You have a verifiable task, math problems, coding problems, and you check whether the final answer is correct. Maybe you add a small format reward so the model puts its reasoning inside the think tags. And that's it. That's the whole signal. And it works surprisingly well, which I think surprised a lot of people, including me.

But there are obvious limitations. The first is that it only works where you can verify the answer. Math and code are nice because you have a ground truth or you can run unit tests. But if you want reasoning for, say, writing a good argument, or planning, or scientific reasoning where the answer isn't a single number, a binary correct-or-not signal doesn't exist. So I think we'll see more work on what people call generative reward models, or LLM-as-a-judge style rewards, where another model grades the quality of the reasoning or the answer along some rubric. The challenge there is reward hacking, of course. The policy model will find whatever the judge likes, and that's not always what you want.

The second thing I'd expect is more process-level rewards, so rewarding intermediate steps rather than just the end. This was the whole process reward model idea from a couple of years back, and interestingly, the DeepSeek team actually reported that it didn't work well for them, partly because it's hard to define what a "good step" is and partly because the reward model gets exploited. But I don't think that's the end of the story. I think the issue was more the implementation than the idea. There's a lot of signal in the chain of thought that we're currently throwing away.

The third one, which I personally find most practical, is efficiency rewards. One of the problems with these models is that they overthink. You ask a simple question and get three thousand tokens of reasoning. So people are experimenting with length penalties, or rewarding the model for solving things in fewer tokens when it can, which is a kind of secondary reward beyond correctness. And that's one where it's actually quite easy to make the signal, you just count tokens, but you have to be careful not to collapse accuracy.

So if I had to summarize: I think correctness stays the backbone because it's the one reward you can really trust, and then these other rewards, process quality, efficiency, judged quality, get layered on top as shaping terms. The open research question is how to combine them without the model gaming the softer ones. And I suspect we'll find, like we did with RLHF, that the reward design ends up mattering more than the RL algorithm itself.

r001.rationale: It says a format reward can make the model put its reasoning inside designated think tags.

r002.rationale: It proposes rewarding the quality of reasoning and intermediate steps, but does not clearly identify the correctness of the reasoning explanation as a distinct reward target.

astra-6.text:
I think final-answer correctness is a very useful starting point because it gives you a relatively clear reward, especially in math or coding. But it doesn’t tell you everything about how the model arrived at that answer. You can get the right answer through a flawed argument, or produce a very long solution when a short one would have been sufficient.

So I expect we’ll see more rewards targeting things like the validity of intermediate steps, efficient use of tools, and knowing when to check an assumption or revise an approach. That could give the model a richer learning signal than simply saying, at the end, “You got it right” or “You got it wrong.”

The challenge is that those properties are harder to evaluate. If you reward something that merely looks like good reasoning, the model may learn to satisfy the evaluator without becoming more reliable. And if you penalize length too aggressively, you might discourage useful exploration.

So my expectation is that these rewards will complement outcome rewards. The interesting question is whether they actually help the model solve new problems more reliably and with less computation, rather than just making its explanations look better.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rewards for intermediate-step validity, but does not state that a formatting reward can train the model to put reasoning in designated tags.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes final-answer correctness from evaluating how the answer was reached, and names the validity of intermediate steps as a separate reward target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think final-answer correctness is a very useful starting point because, especially in math and coding, you can often verify it automatically. But it doesn’t tell you everything about the reasoning. You might get the right answer through a flawed approach, or spend a lot more computation than necessary getting there.

So rewards that capture things like intermediate-step validity, efficiency, or successful tool use could give us a richer training signal. Instead of only learning whether the whole attempt worked, the model gets some feedback about which parts were useful.

The challenge is that those rewards are harder to define. If we reward a particular style of explanation, we might train the model to produce something that looks like good reasoning without actually improving its ability to solve problems. And if another model is judging the steps, we inherit some of that model’s limitations.

My expectation is that we’ll combine these signals: use verifiable outcomes as an anchor, and add other rewards where we can show they improve performance on new problems. I’d be especially interested in whether they help models learn when to keep reasoning, when to check their work, and when they already have enough information to answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rewarding explanation style but does not mention a formatting reward or enclosing reasoning in designated tags.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes final-answer correctness from rewards for intermediate-step validity, identifying reasoning-step correctness as a separate reward target.
